title: Ambition, examined

segments.voice: Yesterday, a tenth: the tithe, zakat and dasvandh, each tradition setting aside a portion. Your line was a share for others. Did a small share leave your hands? Today, the end of the week, and a harder word. Day nine hundred seventeen.

Two brothers walk up to their teacher on the road and ask for a favor before they'll say what it is. In Mark's Gospel they are James and John, fishermen who once left their nets to follow Jesus. The request, when it comes, is blunt: when you come into your glory, let one of us sit at your right hand, and the other at your left. The other ten disciples hear about it, and Mark says they are much displeased with the brothers. Mark doesn't say why. Some readers suspect the ten wanted the same seats. Today's word is the wish that walked up to Jesus on the road: ambition.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS ASK A FAVOR.` → `THE RIGHT HAND AND THE LEFT.` → `THE TEN ARE DISPLEASED.`

segments.voice: Start with what Jesus doesn't do. He doesn't tell them to stop wanting to be great. He calls them to him and turns the ladder upside down. In the King James Bible: "whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister: and whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all." The wish stays. Its direction changes. Ambition isn't erased; it's handed a job. Second, a voice that climbed all the way up. The book of Ecclesiastes speaks as a king in Jerusalem who built houses, planted vineyards, and gathered silver and gold. Then he turns and looks at all of it: "all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun." He reached what he aimed at, and it couldn't tell him what it was for. Third, a teaching from India. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna that his right is to the work itself, never to its fruits; he shouldn't let the fruits be his motive, and he shouldn't cling to doing nothing either. Some readers hear in this a way to strive with everything while loosening the grip on the prize. Fourth, the question all three leave on the table. Ambition can serve, or it can consume, and the difference may lie less in how much someone wants than in what the wanting is for. A promotion that lets someone protect a team is one thing; the same promotion as a scoreboard is another. This week the work days asked how to shape a job, what unpaid work is worth, what we're worth without work, when to stop, how to use money, and what to share. Ambition asks the question under all of them.
screen: `THE GREAT ONE SERVES.` · `NO PROFIT UNDER THE SUN.` · `THE WORK, NOT THE FRUITS.` · `SERVE OR CONSUME?` · then, large: `WHAT IS IT FOR?`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring one ambition to mind, large or small: a job, a number, a finished project, a name on a door. Hold it plainly, without judging it. Now ask it one question: what are you for? Let the first answer come. Then ask the same question of that answer. Keep going, gently, until the answers stop changing. It might end at safety, or love, or someone you want to provide for, or simply wanting to be seen. Any of these can be honest. If you pray, you can hold that last answer in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Ambition. The wish to rise. In Mark's Gospel Jesus doesn't forbid it; he points it toward serving. Today's word.
Your line: what is it for. Today, before you chase the next goal, the next reply, the next number, ask it that question once, and listen to the answer. Day nine hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Christians read Mark 10:43–44 as a teaching that greatness means serving others, and Hindus who study the Bhagavad Gita read 2.47 as guidance on working fully without clinging to the results.
